text:
Chapter Thirty-Six


On paper, Maggie had everything she wanted. The pall was gone. Her office was hers again. Her translation seminar was fully funded. The confirmation email from Edna was sitting in her inbox, with Dean Clearwater copied, outlining the details of the grant. In fact, there was little evidence that Arthur Taliesin had ever been in her office at all.


At some point, Arthur had come to campus and moved his furniture back to storage. He had even returned her desk to its original location, so the only signs of him were the disturbed dust bunnies and that tiny sprig of dried lavender on her bookshelf. And the ache in Maggie’s chest that only seemed to grow with each passing day.


Dahlia curled up on Maggie’s couch, flipping through the same romance novel Maggie had been reading with Arthur. Dahlia hadn’t left Maggie’s side since they dissipated the pall, letting her alternately reason her way through their breakup, cry, and question every decision she’d made. After she had done all that, Dahlia had asked her gently, so gently, if she ought to reconsider.


Maggie had reconsidered. More than once she had been ready to drive out to Atlantia or find Arthur on campus and tell him what really happened in the pall, but she could package up those feelings and put them away. Eventually, the pain would dull. That was what was best for them both. Look at how much she had already upended in the short time they’d known each other.


He needed this job so he could teach and live near his family. She needed it because it was where she had found hers. Neither of them should have to give that up, and isn’t that what would happen if they tried this and it didn’t work? He’s not Evan, she reminded herself. That much had been clear when he apologized outside the pall. Evan would never admit he was wrong, not even over small things. But she was still Maggie.


No, she couldn’t do that to him. And if that meant she had to suck it up and see Arthur Taliesin in a faculty meeting once a month without remembering the way he made her feel treasured, perfect—she could do it. She could. It didn’t matter if she loved him, and, gods below, she did.


“You can’t sweep away the summer, babe,” Dahlia said as Maggie swept at the same spot on the floor for the third time.


Maggie glared at her and Dahlia shrugged, turning the page in her book. “Maybe I need a mop.”


“I don’t think that’s what you need either.” Dahlia rested her book on the back of the fainting couch, and Maggie winced, knowing that her friend was about to pick holes in all of her arguments for why she couldn’t tell Arthur Taliesin the truth.


A knock interrupted them, and Maggie looked at the door with her heart beating ferociously as she said, “Come in.” She wanted to see his dark hair with the shots of gray, his honey eyes, and his broad shoulders, but she deflated when Dean Clearwater opened the door.


“Maggie, I need to speak with you.” He looked pointedly at Dahlia.


“I’m gonna go get you that mop,” Dahlia said, giving Maggie’s shoulder a squeeze as she scooted past the dean.


Maggie gestured to the spot on the couch that Dahlia had vacated, and he sat down. He didn’t wait for Maggie to get settled before he said, “What happened? When we spoke, you promised me there was nothing I needed to know.”


Maggie suddenly felt faint. She didn’t know what the dean was talking about. “I—what—what do you mean?”


“What happened?” he repeated.


“All that has happened since we spoke is that Ar—Dr. Taliesin and I dissipated the pall,” Maggie said, treading carefully. Until she knew exactly why the dean was upset, she didn’t want to incriminate herself.


“Then why did Dr. Taliesin turn in his resignation this morning?”


“What?” Did Maggie hear him properly? “What do you mean?”


The dean held out the piece of paper he’d scrunched in his fist. She took it gingerly and opened the letter, recognizing the loopy A and T in Arthur’s signature. She managed to read only the first line before the words began to swim.



This letter serves as notification that I, Arthur Taliesin, am resigning my position at Hawthorn College, effective immediately…



Maggie sat down in her desk chair, letting it slide back against the bookshelf with a small thud. “This leaves us in a very precarious position. Who is going to teach his Materials Alchemy courses? The term starts in a few weeks!”


“I had no idea.” Maggie looked away from the dean, biting her lip.


“Was there some sort of problem? Does this have anything to do with the grant?”


“No. There was no problem,” she said quickly, knowing it wasn’t true. This was what she had tried so desperately to avoid, and it was happening anyway.


She stared at the letter, sentences jumping out at her.



I apologize for the short notice. Please let me know if there is anything I can do to help fill the position. I have several former grad students who would be great additions to the Hawthorn faculty that I’d be pleased to recommend…



She needed to do something. She couldn’t let him throw away his chance to have the exact career he wanted near his family. And if he left Hawthorn…At least, if they were colleagues, she would still get to see him, even if it hurt. That was better than never seeing him again. When she thought about that possibility, the pressure in her chest became unbearable and she couldn’t breathe.


“I’ll fix this,” Maggie said to the dean, ripping Arthur’s resignation letter in half before throwing it in the trash. She looked over at the clock. “Is he still on campus?”


“He dropped this off an hour ago. He told me he’d be helping the custodial staff clear out the pall remnants on the third floor. Check there—”


Maggie didn’t wait for Dean Clearwater to finish talking. She left her office and sprinted up the stairs.



—


Maggie should have walked, because she was out of breath by the time she made it to the alchemy labs. The third floor of Ilex Hall was still covered in pall slime, sludge, and dust. Equipment was still strewn everywhere, and there were student and teacher belongings that still needed to be claimed on every table. This floor had been a flurry of activity as custodial staff, faculty volunteers, and the tech team worked to clear it out and salvage equipment, but now the only sound was coming from Arthur’s alchemy lab.


She tried to catch her breath. They hadn’t seen each other since they dissipated the pall. Long days of silence, of picking up her phone and putting it down without sending him a message, of trying to figure out a way to take it all back before convincing herself it had been the right thing to do. But now that he was almost in front of her, she could admit how much she missed him.


She caught a glimpse of him through the door into his lab. He stood on a ladder, his sleeves pushed up to his elbows, and dipped a sponge in a bucket of water. As he cleaned the window, streaks of sunlight came through the now-clear glass and hit his hair, highlighting the shots of silvery gray. He was covered in dust and pall slime, but he was still so stupidly handsome. Maggie wanted to call out to him, but her voice was stuck in her throat. She wanted to take a step forward into the lab, but she couldn’t do it.


It was Arthur who turned around to see her. Slowly, he dropped the sponge back in his bucket and dried his hands on the old jeans he was wearing. He jumped down from the ladder and lifted a hand in an awkward greeting before saying, “Hi.”


She wanted to run to him. She wanted to say sorry, a thousand times, and then kiss him until he was sick of her. Instead, Maggie couldn’t stop the words that spilled out of her. “You can’t leave,” she sputtered.


He crossed his arms and leaned against one of the cleaner tables. “Why not?”


“You need a job! You need a job here, at Hawthorn,” she rattled on. “You can’t leave Rory and Simon now. And I can’t be—I won’t be—responsible for breaking up your family because you need to find a university job somewhere else.” She was rambling and pacing as he stood watching her with frustrating amusement. “Do you know how rare it is to find an academic job near the place you want to live? It’s impossible! Why would you throw that away?”


“I think you know, Maggie,” he said.


He was putting her in an impossible position—she didn’t want him to have to choose between her and his job. She had left him so that he never had to make this decision at all, and he’d quit anyway. That wasn’t what she wanted. It wasn’t what she’d asked for. If he had just talked to her before doing this absurd thing, he’d know that.


There was a small, careful smile on his face. The one that seemed to say he knew her better than she knew herself. He took a step toward her, but Maggie stepped back and her face heated. “Did you think this would make me change my mind?”


“No,” he answered simply.


“Is this supposed to make me fall for you? Some kind of grand gesture?”


“I think,” he began, “you’ve already fallen.”


Maggie screwed up her face and was ready to argue when Arthur went on. “It’s okay if you’re not ready to admit it. It’s okay if you still need space. I’m not expecting anything.” His voice was so soft, so tentative, as he went on. “But I’d be an absolute fool to let something stupid like a job stand in the way of whatever this is between us.”


“You’re throwing this away because I might like you?”


“Would you say you like like me?” he asked, that grin quirking up again. She never should have told him about that conversation.


“Arthur,” she groaned, throwing up her hands.


“Maggie,” he replied gently. “I’m Arthur Taliesin. I can get a job wherever I want, doing whatever I want.”


“Oh, shut up,” she said under her breath, rolling her eyes. Above and below, he was so conceited when he wanted to be. His smile widened as she kept going, punctuating each argument with a jab of her finger into her palm. “You love this job. I’ve seen you in your classroom, the way you light up around your students. You love teaching here. What would possess you to give that up?”


Arthur looked at her thoughtfully. “I didn’t know you noticed,” he said quietly.


Somehow this made her even angrier. At him. At herself. She wasn’t sure which. “Of course I noticed! You think I don’t see you the same way you see me?”


His fingers flexed, and he looked like he wanted to take another step forward, but he hesitated. “You’re right, I do love teaching. But it doesn’t matter where I do it.”


Had he really quit his job for her? It was ridiculous. Maggie was used to chasing certainties. She made decisions after mapping every possible outcome and feeling satisfied with all of them. But Arthur had just leaped off the building without so much as a soft place to land.


“What if this doesn’t work out?” she asked frantically. “What if you give this up for me and I’m not who you think I am? What if we fight all the time and you can’t stand me?”


“Then it doesn’t work out. Maggie, I’m not giving up a lifelong dream. It’s a job.” He paused and then frowned before asking, “Maggie, what happened in the pall?”


Did he remember? She tried to stall. “What do you mean?”


“I was ready to let you go,” he admitted, stepping just a little bit closer to Maggie. “I was. But then I started to make sense of everything that happened. It became clearer which memories belonged to the unsettled dead and which ones were mine.” He watched her intently as she bit her lip, but then he closed his eyes and his voice sounded so broken when he asked, “Were you just telling me what I wanted to hear?”


Gods below, how could she have ever made him feel that way? She swallowed, her eyes welling up with tears, and she shook her head. “No,” she rasped. “No, I wasn’t, but…”


Maggie looked away from the hope in his expression, hope she knew was mirrored in her own chest, which was holding a heart that beat too much and too fast. Arthur took another step forward, and, this time, Maggie didn’t back up. Tentatively, he closed the gap even more, the distance between them narrowing until he could reach out and touch her.


Just as she was about to close that small distance left between them, she came back to her senses. She backed up again and said sharply, “You can’t do things like this without talking to me about it. Quitting your job, Arthur?”


For the first time, something like anger flashed across his expression. His words were only laced in bitterness, but it was enough to knock the breath out of her. “Do friends who fuck need to run career decisions by each other?” She winced as he threw her own words back at her. Had she really said those awful things to him?


“I didn’t—”


“Tell me,” he said suddenly, all the bitterness gone and replaced with pure need. “Tell me you don’t want this.”


Lie to him, came a traitorous voice in her head, but she could no more lie to Arthur now than she could that first day they kissed. “I can’t,” she whispered.


“You can’t what, Maggie? Please be specific.”


She closed her eyes, squeezing her hand against her thigh. She wished she could lie to him; it would be easier than cracking her chest open so thoroughly. “I can’t tell you that, because I can’t lie to you.” She paused. “I won’t.” Then, in a small, pleading voice, she said, “I want you to say it.” She didn’t deserve it, but she wanted to hear it all the same.


He smiled, and he was so handsome, his face alight with a happiness that thrilled and terrified her. “I love you, Maggie Linden.” Her heart was beating so fast, she thought it might come out of her chest. She could barely breathe as his words settled on her skin, as soft and warm as his jacket. “I love you more than this job, and I am not content with a summer fling. I want all of you. Always.” He stepped closer and closer with each word, the few feet between them suddenly nothing. “And I understand if you aren’t ready for that. I don’t…” He searched for the words. “I don’t expect anything of you. But if the fact that we are both employed by Hawthorn College is the reason you want to throw this away, then I am no longer employed by Hawthorn College.”


The silence stretched as they stared at each other. Arthur had stopped when there was about a foot left between them, unwilling to make the final move to close the remaining space, like he was convinced it had to be her. So she took a single step forward, reached up, and brushed a stray dollop of pall slime off his cheekbone. Her hand cupped his cheek, and he leaned into her touch. She felt, inexplicably, like crying.


“I ripped up your resignation letter and threw it in the trash,” she said with a hiccup that devolved into a full laugh. “I told Dean Clearwater I wouldn’t let you quit.”


Arthur brought his hand up to hers on his cheek and gripped her palm, narrowing his eyes with confusion. “Why would you do that?”


“Because Dean Clearwater warned me back in May that I had better not scare you off,” she explained, and again her words were punctuated by a kind of hysterical laughter that she couldn’t quite control. “You are much too important to the future of Hawthorn. He heavily implied that my tenure application might be in trouble, too. Of course, almost immediately after he told me that, I went back to our office and picked a fight with you.”


“I’ll be having a conversation with Dean Clearwater this afternoon, it seems.” His expression softened. “Why didn’t you tell me?”


Maggie shrugged. “You’ve been very distracting.” Her voice was husky, and she was staring at his lips. “Say it again, please.”


He dipped his head until she could almost feel the flutter of his mouth on hers. “I love you, Maggie.”


She leaned forward and kissed him, letting his mouth catch her moan. Missing him had been a painful ache. She broke the kiss and said so quietly it was nearly a whisper, like she was telling him a secret, “I’m sorry for what I said. It has never been true, and I regretted it the moment the words were out of my mouth.” He brushed back a piece of her hair, his fingertips trailing behind her ear and down her neck.


“I have been lying to myself for a long time. I think I’ve known since the day you carried me out of the pall,” she admitted, as much to herself as to Arthur. “You were so tender and so kind, and I was such a mess. And then you called Dahlia to take care of me. And, every day since, I have just been trying to convince myself that what I felt wasn’t that.


“Dahlia called me a coward, you know,” she said. “Because I couldn’t admit it even to her.”


“Admit what, Maggie?”


“That I love you, too.”


Every one of his tentative touches became insistent as he pulled her toward him, wrapping his arms around her waist, gripping the hem of her shirt in his long fingers. He inhaled as he held her, breathing her in. And she was mesmerized by the way their bodies still fit together like she was exactly where she was supposed to be. He tipped her head back and kissed her, long, languid, slow. It was not an urgent kiss. It was a kiss for people who had time.


“I’m so sorry,” she said again. “I was—I am scared.”


“I know,” he whispered, kissing her forehead with a gentle tenderness that Maggie had never known before.


In the time since she had told Arthur they were done, during one of her many, many conversations with Dahlia, she had grown so exhausted of letting Evan and his betrayal occupy so much of her present. “It wasn’t fair of me to treat you like your mistake was remotely like what Evan did to me,” she said. “I was mad, I was worried about my job, but what you did wasn’t anything like what he did.”


He wrapped her in an embrace, and they held each other, neither one of them wanting to let the other go. After a moment, Maggie said, “Let’s go find Dean Clearwater and get your job back.” She knew, without a doubt, that she didn’t care anymore. They would find a way to make it work. If their love didn’t last, they were adults. And what if it did last?


Arthur looked thoughtful for a moment. “I think,” he began carefully, “resigning from my position at Hawthorn is one of the only things I’ve been sure of in a long time.” His hand brushed her hair as he went on, “Other than how I feel about you, that is.”


She flushed. He had always been so sure. Even from the moment of that very first kiss, when he’d wanted to remove their masks on Beltane. “You’re quitting anyway?”


He held her hand, rubbing her palm with his thumb. “For years now, I’ve been unhappy. It didn’t start when my mom died, but after, I couldn’t ignore it anymore. I don’t think it was until I got to Hawthorn, though, that I realized the problem wasn’t Dartwood. I’m tired of the politics, of people thinking my name is worth more than anything else I bring to the school. I’m done.” Then he said softly, “But I wish you had told me about what the dean said. I would have gone about things a little differently.”


“I’m sorry,” she said softly.


“I think I know a way to make Dean Clearwater happy, though. Even if I don’t teach Materials Alchemy next semester. What do you think?”


“I think I love you, Arthur Taliesin.”


And then they were kissing again. They might have kissed for a minute or five, Maggie was never sure. Time was lost with Arthur’s lips on hers, with his hands in her hair. She tugged him closer, closer by the dusty fabric of his shirt, wrapping her arms around him. She had almost lost him. Almost lost this. Maggie was tired of letting past hurts rule her life. She was done with all of that.


Instead, Maggie was choosing Arthur, and Arthur had long ago chosen her.
